source.title: Sketched Linear Contrastive Learning: Approximation, Optimization, and Statistical Scaling
source.authors: Zi-Yang Chen; Zhong-Zhu Zhou; Ding-Xuan Zhou

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Derives and synthetically evaluates scaling and compute-allocation results in a new setting: a sketched bilinear contrastive-learning model, rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper's references to empirical scaling results for language, vision, and other areas are background citations, not results from this study. Its own results concern a theoretical paired-Gaussian contrastive model and synthetic experiments.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper on an idealized sketched bilinear contrastive model with Gaussian views. It borrows the scaling-law framing and the Kaplan/Hoffmann-style compute proxy (C ≍ LNM²). Its synthetic experiments only check its own theorem, and the power-law spectra are assumed (Assumption 1), so the power-law rates follow from those assumptions. Nothing measures the loss of a trained language, image, video or other deployed model. So no result bears on whether any version holds for real systems. V3: the allocation exponents are derived heuristics for this toy objective and are never compared with measured compute-optimal runs. V5: a linear Gaussian surrogate is not another modality or training regime of the kind V5 names. V7: the bending curve is the GD-variance component, which bends exactly as the paper's own piecewise formula predicts. It is not a total-loss curve departing from a single power law, and fitting choices are not varied. The reader's 'tests/T3' is not accepted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that sketched bilinear contrastive learning scales differently from sketched linear regression, because finite-sample noise is governed by a product effective dimension over spectral-direction pairs. Combined with C ≍ LNM², this gives regime-dependent allocation heuristics: in covariance-limited regimes data just suffices for covariance control, while variance-balanced regimes need extra paired data. They present the synthetic experiments as qualitative support for their own theorem. They call the model idealized rather than a quantitative description of CLIP-style scaling.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical and synthetic study of a Gaussian bilinear contrastive objective trained with full-batch GD, not an empirical language-model pretraining scaling sweep. It uses a compute proxy C ≍ LNM² and derives allocation heuristics under spectral and covariance assumptions.
record.method_sensitivity: The allocation exponents depend on the regime indexed by q and b; the variance curve has distinct early, intermediate, and late slopes. The theoretical results also require spectral-alignment/source conditions and a covariance-control regime.

fits_no_version.finding: In a sketched bilinear Gaussian contrastive model, approximation error and GD bias follow theorem-predicted power laws in sketch dimension and optimization horizon (synthetic slopes −2.01 vs −2.00 and −0.86 vs −0.91). The GD variance grows with a 'product effective dimension' over pairs of spectral directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical toy-model derivations of scaling laws: assumed power-law data spectra produce power-law risk components in tractable linear and contrastive models.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the proxy C ≍ LNM², the derived compute-optimal exponents for model dimension, paired data and horizon change with the source smoothness regime (forced unsaturated, covariance-limited, variance-balanced).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical compute-allocation exponents in tractable models are regime-dependent (theory only, no empirical runs).

record.problems: The evidence is for an idealized synthetic model, not practical language or multimodal models. The authors note the bilinear matched-view formulation, absence of explicit sampled negatives, Gaussian data, full-batch GD, and strong covariance-control assumptions. The allocation result is explicitly a heuristic, logarithmic factors are suppressed, and no uncertainty intervals are reported for the experimental slopes or values.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: All; no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All; no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All empirically; the allocation rules are theory-only heuristics for a toy objective.
All; no real image, video, contrastive (e.g. CLIP) or other-regime model is trained or measured.
All; no fitting-choice, schedule or parameter-counting comparison, and no total-loss curve departing from a power law.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3/V5/V7 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are withdrawn. The rows verify the paper's own theorems in a synthetic model whose power-law spectra are assumed, and the optimization experiments replace empirical marginal covariances with controlled perturbed population covariances. Relation could alternatively be 'discusses'/T6. 'uses_without_test'/T4 was chosen because the paper relies on the scaling-law compute-proxy framing as its tool. No uncertainty is reported on the fitted slopes.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.stage_stated: population sketched moments; no finite-dataset training
rows.operation_detail: Varied sketch dimension and measured approximation error.
rows.measure: Fitted log-log slope of approximation error versus sketch dimension
rows.locator: Section 4; Supplementary Material G, Approximation experiment
rows.note: The paper says the empirical approximation curve closely follows the predicted rate.
rows.check: Checks the paper's own approximation-rate theorem (slope −2.01 vs predicted −2.00). The rate follows from the assumed power-law spectra and spectral-truncation sketch. It is computed from population moments, not from a trained model's held-out loss. No claim version is measured.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of GD iterations and measured GD bias against accumulated stepsize ΓL.
rows.measure: Fitted log-log slope of GD bias versus ΓL
rows.locator: Section 4; Supplementary Material G, GD-bias experiment
rows.note: The measured bias is reported to decrease throughout the tested horizon.
rows.check: GD-bias slope (−0.86 vs −0.91) checks the paper's own Theorem 1. Marginal covariances were replaced by controlled perturbed population covariances, not raw empirical ones (Supp. G). This is not a loss-scaling measurement of any model class in V5.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Measured GD variance across independently sampled datasets as the iteration count varied.
rows.measure: Fitted log-log slope of GD variance versus optimization horizon
rows.locator: Section 4; Supplementary Material G, GD-variance experiment
rows.note: The paper describes near-linear growth on the early log-log scale.
rows.check: Early-segment slope of the GD-variance component, which grows with optimization time as the paper's own theory predicts. It is not a loss curve versus parameters, data or compute, so V5 and V7 do not apply. No baseline is stated.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Measured GD variance across independently sampled datasets as the iteration count varied.
rows.measure: Fitted log-log slope of GD variance versus optimization horizon
rows.locator: Section 4; Supplementary Material G, GD-variance experiment
rows.note: The lower slope than in the early segment is part of the reported bending curve.
rows.check: The 'partial' state is wrong: the intermediate slope of 0.71 is the bending the paper's own finite-filter reference predicts, not a weaker effect. It measures the variance component, not loss, so it gives no evidence on V7's fit-dependence or a bending loss law.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Measured GD variance across independently sampled datasets as the iteration count varied.
rows.measure: Fitted log-log slope of GD variance versus optimization horizon
rows.locator: Section 4; Supplementary Material G, GD-variance experiment
rows.note: The paper says the curve bends and has not flattened into a saturated plateau over the tested range.
rows.check: Same as r4. The late slope of 0.42 is the predicted bending of the variance component and should not be scored 'partial' against any version.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical excess risk with the bias-plus-variance reference across optimization checkpoints.

conditions.value: same optimization checkpoints as the other optimization panels

rows.measure: Maximum relative discrepancy between empirical excess risk and bias-plus-variance reference
rows.locator: Section 4; Supplementary Material G, Excess-risk decomposition experiment
rows.note: The study reports that empirical excess risk is nearly identical to the reference curve.
rows.check: Validates the paper's own risk decomposition: the cross term is below 0.6% of the bias-plus-variance reference. This is internal method verification, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Measured empirical excess risk at the reported minimum.
rows.locator: Supplementary Material G, Excess-risk decomposition experiment
rows.note: The paper describes the curve as U-shaped, with its minimum near this point.
rows.check: A single excess-risk value at the U-shaped minimum (L≈768), with no scaling baseline. It is an overfitting-in-time point, not evidence on any version.

rows.subject: paired Gaussian latent-variable sketched bilinear contrastive model
rows.operation_detail: Measured empirical excess risk at the final reported optimization checkpoint.
rows.locator: Supplementary Material G, Excess-risk decomposition experiment
rows.note: The paper says the curve rises after the bias reduction phase as variance dominates.
rows.check: A single excess-risk value at the final checkpoint, with no baseline. It shows the variance-dominated rise, which is not a scaling-law measurement.

rows.subject: sketched bilinear contrastive-learning model
rows.size_stated: M is sketch dimension; N is paired sample size
rows.operation_detail: Derived allocation powers under C ≍ LNM², ignoring logarithmic factors and taking γ ≍ 1.

rows.check: A derived heuristic exponent, not a measured result. The authors say this forced case is not the unconstrained optimum. Nothing compares it with actual compute-optimal runs.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The paper's stated compute proxy and each of the three specified allocation regimes
reader_labels.reason: The derived rules give power-law growth of model dimension and paired data with compute in each regime (r9–r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Allocation outside a single fixed regime or outside the theorem's assumptions
reader_labels.reason: The exponents differ by regime, and the authors identify Proposition 2 as a heuristic rather than a minimax optimality theorem (r9–r11).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The tested synthetic paired-Gaussian, sketched bilinear contrastive setup
reader_labels.reason: Approximation and GD bias follow their predicted power-law slopes, and the excess-risk decomposition is closely matched in the experiment (r1, r2, r6–r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Applying the result to practical multimodal or language-model pretraining
reader_labels.reason: The study itself describes the model as idealized and notes its bilinear matched-view, Gaussian, full-batch, and covariance-control assumptions (r1–r2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GD-variance curve over the tested early, intermediate, and late horizon segments
reader_labels.reason: The reported variance slopes change from approximately 1.04 to 0.71 to 0.42, and the curve bends without reaching a plateau over the tested range (r3–r5).
